learn.hook: That embarrassing comment from Class 8 could show up when a college or employer searches your name. The internet has a long memory.
points: Digital technology makes banking, learning and communication faster and easier, but the same tools can be misused, so we must use them responsibly.
A digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind while using the internet: posts, searches, sites visited, purchases, location and more.
Active digital footprint: data you share intentionally, such as posts, comments, emails, uploaded photos and online forms you fill.
Passive digital footprint: data collected without you actively sharing it, such as browsing history, cookies, IP address, app usage and location tracking.

Footprints are stored on your device (browser history, cookies) and on remote servers of websites and apps. Even after you delete a post, copies may remain, so footprints are very hard to erase completely.

example.q: Classify: (a) a reel you posted, (b) a shopping site remembering what you viewed, (c) a review you wrote, (d) your phone's location history.
steps: (a) Posted on purpose → active
(b) Recorded through cookies while browsing → passive
(c) Written on purpose → active
(d) Collected in the background → passive
example.answer: Active: a, c. Passive: b, d.

learn.reallife: Recruiters and college admission teams sometimes look at applicants' public social media. A thoughtful online presence can open doors; a careless one can close them.

learn.hook: In a group chat of 200 classmates, one rude forward can ruin everyone's day. Being a good netizen is about small, everyday choices.
points: A digital society uses digital technology in every part of life. A netizen (internet + citizen) is anyone who uses the internet; a responsible netizen follows safe, ethical and legal practices.

Net etiquette: Be ethical (don't violate copyright; share your expertise), be respectful (respect privacy and diversity of opinions, cultures and backgrounds), be responsible (avoid cyberbullying; don't feed the trolls, i.e. ignore provocative posts).

Communication etiquette (email, chat, comments): be precise (respect others' time and data limits; don't send huge unnecessary files), be polite, and be credible (think before you comment). Avoid spam and mass forwards.
Social media etiquette: be secure (strong passwords, know who you befriend, beware of fake news and fake profiles) and be reliable (think before uploading: posts and photos may stay online for ever).

example.q: Classify each: (a) ignoring a troll's insulting comment, (b) forwarding unverified news, (c) crediting a photographer when sharing their picture, (d) accepting requests from unknown profiles.
steps: (a) Don't feed the trolls → good (be responsible)
(b) Spreading possible fake news → bad (be secure/reliable)
(c) Respecting the creator's rights → good (be ethical)
(d) Not knowing who you befriend → bad (be secure)
example.answer: Good: a, c. Bad: b, d.

learn.reallife: During exam results season, fake 'CBSE result links' spread on WhatsApp. A responsible netizen checks the official website before forwarding anything.

topics.title: Data protection, intellectual property and licences

learn.hook: The song you're humming, the logo on your shoes and the medicine your grandmother takes are all protected by intellectual property laws.
points: Data protection keeps sensitive personal data (bank details, health records, passwords, Aadhaar) safe through encryption, authentication (passwords, OTPs, biometrics) and data-protection laws.

Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) protect creations of the mind. Copyright protects creative and literary work (books, music, software code, films). A patent protects an invention, usually for about 20 years. A trademark protects a brand's name, logo or symbol.

Violations: plagiarism (presenting someone else's work as your own without credit), copyright infringement (using protected work without permission), trademark infringement (using another's mark without permission).

Public-access licences let creators share work: Creative Commons (CC) for creative content; GNU GPL and Apache for software. FOSS (Free and Open Source Software) lets users use, study, modify and share code.
Software piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution or use of software, and is illegal.

example.q: Classify: (a) copying a blog post into your project without credit, (b) a startup using a logo almost identical to a famous brand's, (c) selling copied DVDs of a new film.
steps: (a) Using another's words as your own → plagiarism
(b) Misusing a brand's mark → trademark infringement
(c) Distributing protected work without permission → copyright infringement (piracy)

learn.reallife: Indian generic drug makers can produce a medicine once its patent expires. Meanwhile, Bollywood producers fight film piracy because every pirated copy is lost revenue.

topics.title: Cyber crime: hacking, phishing, ransomware and bullying

learn.hook: 'Your KYC has expired. Click here to update or your account will be blocked.' Thousands of Indians lose money to messages like this every year.
points: Cyber crime is any criminal activity in which a computer or network is used as a tool, a target, or both.

Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system. Ethical (white hat) hackers are authorised to find security weaknesses so they can be fixed; non-ethical (black hat) hackers break in to steal, damage or demand money.

Phishing: fake emails, SMSes or websites that look genuine trick people into revealing passwords, OTPs or card details. Email spoofing fakes the sender's address. Identity theft uses stolen personal details for fraud: financial (bank fraud), criminal (committing crimes in another's name) or medical (claiming treatment).
Ransomware encrypts the victim's files and demands payment (ransom) to unlock them. It spreads through malicious email attachments, fake downloads and infected websites or networks.
Eavesdropping: secretly intercepting communication on a network. Cyber trolls post provocative comments to upset people. Cyberbullying is using digital media to harass, threaten or humiliate someone.

example.q: A student gets an email from 'support@paypa1-secure.com' asking for an OTP to 'stop a payment'. Identify the crime and the red flags.
steps: The sender's address is a fake look-alike ('paypa1' uses the digit 1 in place of 'l'), made to pass as a trusted sender (spoofing)
It creates panic and urgency
It asks for an OTP, which no genuine company ever asks for
This is phishing aimed at financial identity theft

learn.reallife: The 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack hit systems in many countries, including India. And the national cyber-crime helpline 1930 receives calls daily about UPI and KYC phishing scams.

topics.title: Cyber safety, malware and preventing cyber crime

learn.hook: A free 'game hack' app asks for access to your SMS and contacts. That's not a game; that could be a trojan.
points: Cyber safety means using the internet safely: browsing only trusted (HTTPS) sites, protecting your identity (not over-sharing personal details), and keeping information confidential (never sharing passwords or OTPs).

Malware (malicious software) types: a virus attaches itself to files or programs and spreads when they are run; a worm copies itself across networks on its own; a trojan pretends to be useful software but harms the system; spyware secretly collects your information; adware shows unwanted advertisements.

Prevention: take regular backups; use and update antivirus software; keep the OS and apps updated; use strong, different passwords and two-factor authentication; check for HTTPS and the padlock icon; don't open unknown attachments or links.
Digital signatures verify that a document or email really comes from the claimed sender and hasn't been altered.
Report cyber crime to the local cyber cell, the national portal cybercrime.gov.in, or the helpline 1930 for financial frauds.

example.q: Make a strong password from the idea 'I love cricket since 2015'.
steps: Weak: 'cricket' or '123456' (easy to guess)
Use initials, numbers, symbols and mixed case: 'Ilc$2015!'
Make it long and unique to this account
Turn on two-factor authentication too

learn.reallife: When you pay on an e-commerce site, the 'https://' and padlock mean the connection is encrypted, and your bank's OTP adds a second layer of authentication.

learn.hook: India has a law for the online world and rules for the old phones in your drawer. Both protect citizens, one from crime and one from toxins.
points: The Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act), amended in 2008, gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, making e-commerce and e-governance legally valid.

It lays down provisions and penalties for cyber crimes such as hacking, identity theft and publishing obscene material online. Cyber cells in police departments investigate such crimes, and the Act provided for a Cyber Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals.
E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment: old phones, computers, batteries, TVs, chargers. It contains harmful substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium.
Dumping or burning e-waste releases toxins into soil, water and air, harming the health of people (especially informal workers) and the environment.

Proper management: Reduce (buy only what you need, use devices longer), Reuse (repair, donate or resell working devices), Recycle (give e-waste to authorised collection centres or recyclers, not the regular garbage).

example.q: Your family has an old laptop, a dead phone battery and a working but outdated tablet. What should you do with each?
steps: Working tablet → reuse: donate it to a school or someone who needs it
Old laptop → wipe data, then sell back or give to an authorised e-waste recycler
Dead battery → drop at an authorised collection point; never throw it in household garbage or burn it
example.answer: Reuse what works; send the rest to authorised e-waste collection

learn.reallife: India generates a large and growing amount of e-waste every year. Many brands now run take-back schemes, and authorised recyclers safely recover metals like copper and gold.

topics.title: Health, ergonomics and technology for everyone

learn.hook: Hours of online classes and scrolling can leave you with dry eyes, a stiff neck and poor sleep. Technology should fit you, not the other way round.
points: Overuse of devices can cause eye strain (dry, tired eyes), poor posture and back or neck pain, repetitive stress injuries in wrists and fingers, sleep problems, and internet addiction.

Ergonomics is designing and arranging workspaces and devices to fit the user: screen at or slightly below eye level and about an arm's length away, back supported, feet flat on the floor, wrists straight.

Healthy habits: take regular breaks (e.g. the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds), keep screens away before bedtime, and clean devices and keyboards regularly.

Gender issues: girls are sometimes discouraged from computing; schools should give equal access and encouragement. Disability issues: students with disabilities need assistive technology such as screen readers, Braille keyboards, speech-to-text software and screen magnifiers.
Exam-style tasks: classify scenarios (plagiarism, hacking, phishing), compare copyright and patent, analyse etiquette, and recall IT Act provisions.

example.q: Riya studies on her bed with her laptop on her lap for 3 hours. Suggest ergonomic fixes.
steps: Use a table and chair with back support
Raise the screen to eye level (a stand or books)
Keep feet flat and wrists straight
Take a short break every 20–30 minutes and follow the 20-20-20 rule
example.answer: Proper desk setup plus regular breaks

learn.reallife: Screen-reader software and Indian-language text-to-speech tools help visually impaired students study and appear in exams, while initiatives that bring more girls into coding are narrowing the gender gap in tech.

quiz.q: Ergonomics is the study of:
options: Designing workplaces and devices to fit the user comfortably and safely
quiz.explain: Ergonomics aims to reduce strain and injury by fitting tools to people.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it's about computer performance

quiz.q: Which practice reduces eye strain?
options: Holding the phone very close to the eyes
Using the screen in a dark room at full brightness
quiz.explain: Regular distant focusing gives the eye muscles a rest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks brighter screens are always better

quiz.q: Pain in the wrists from long hours of typing and mouse use is an example of:
quiz.explain: Repeating the same motions for long periods strains muscles and tendons.
quiz.mistake: Confuses physical strain with other issues

quiz.q: Which is the correct position for a monitor?
options: At or slightly below eye level, about an arm's length away
quiz.explain: This keeps the neck neutral and reduces eye strain.
quiz.mistake: Thinks closer screens are clearer and better

quiz.q: A screen reader helps:
options: Visually impaired users by reading out the text on the screen
quiz.explain: Screen readers convert on-screen text to speech or Braille.
quiz.mistake: Doesn't know assistive technologies

quiz.q: Which step promotes gender equality in a school computer lab?
options: Assuming girls are not interested in programming
Allowing only boys to join the coding club
Giving girls and boys equal access, time and encouragement to use computers
quiz.explain: Equal access and encouragement address the gender gap in computing.
quiz.mistake: Accepts stereotypes about who can code

quiz.q: Case: A student copies code from a website into a project without credit, and another breaks into the school server. Classify the two acts.
quiz.explain: Using someone's code as your own is plagiarism; unauthorised access to a server is hacking.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the categories of cyber misconduct

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Using a phone in bed late at night can disturb sleep.
Reason (R): Screen use before bedtime keeps the brain alert and delays sleep.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Late screen use stimulates the brain and pushes sleep later, explaining A.
quiz.mistake: Doesn't connect screen use with sleep

teach.ask: Gappu's neck hurts after online classes. Explain the health effects of overusing devices, ergonomics, and how tech can include everyone.
teach.praise: Bad posture and long screen hours cause strain, so ergonomics and breaks help. And assistive tech plus equal access make computing fair for everyone!
teach.nudge: Good. What health problems come from overuse, and what does ergonomics suggest?
